title: three things, out loud, badly
tomorrow: the rule that keeps turning up

lines: THE FOOD, THE WI-FI, THE DOG.
cards: Family dinner. Somebody says, okay, everyone name one thing you're thankful for. Half the table groans.
Somebody says the food. Somebody says Wi-Fi. A kid says the dog.
It's awkward, it's a bit forced, and it's over in a minute. That clumsy minute may be worth more than it looks. Today asks for three things.
Out loud. Badly. Not eloquent, not the perfect list.

teach.b: Start with the emperor from day three. Marcus Aurelius's private notebook doesn't open with philosophy at all, at least as it comes down to us. It opens with a list of thank-yous.
From his grandfather, good morals and an even temper. From his mother, generosity, and a simple way of living. Teacher after teacher, friend after friend, what each one gave him.
A man who ruled an empire starts by counting what he'd been given.
Paul, writing to a young church, tells them, in old English wording: "In every thing give thanks." Notice he doesn't say for everything. In everything.
Inside whatever is happening, find something to thank. Jewish tradition has a short prayer, the Modeh Ani, said on waking, while still in bed, thanking God for giving back the soul for another day.

teach.h: THANKS BEFORE GETTING OUT OF BED.
teach.b: Thanks comes first, before coffee, before news. And then the lab.

teach.h: WRITE IT DOWN, NO FEELING REQUIRED.
teach.b: In 2003 the psychologists Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough asked some people to write down, each week, a few things they were grateful for, while others wrote about hassles or ordinary events.

After ten weeks, the gratitude group rated their lives as a whole more highly and felt more hopeful about the week ahead. Nobody was asked to feel grateful first. They were only asked to write it down.
That's why badly is allowed. Gratitude isn't a mood you wait for. It's a thing you say, and on hard days you say it anyway.
The Stoic Seneca kept an evening version: once the lamp was out, he went back over his day. So if you keep a journal and wonder what to write, here's a pair. In the morning: what matters today?
At night: what went well, and what would I do differently?

how: Many people keep a short gratitude practice: a few things written in a notebook each night, a thanksgiving said at meals, or, in Jewish tradition, a brief prayer of thanks said on waking.

games.q: you're Marcus Aurelius, emperor of Rome, opening a private notebook. how do you begin?
o: with a list of your victories.
with a list of what other people gave you.
games.why: book one of the Meditations thanks his grandfather, his mother, his teachers and friends, one by one.

practice: Here's the practice, and yes, it's out loud. If you're somewhere you can't speak, whisper it, or just move your lips. Name three things you're thankful for right now, the first three that come.
They can be tiny: warm socks, a text from someone, the bus that came. Say them badly. Then, for about forty-five seconds, sit with the third one and let it land.

wordCard.voice: Gratitude. Noticing what you've been given, and saying so, even before the feeling arrives. Fourteenth word. Thoughts, body, sit, the phone, silence, enough, gratitude: that's week two.

orig.note: Latin: favor, kindness, and thanks. English gratitude and grace both come from the same family (gratus, pleasing).

carryVoice: Your line: thank you anyway. It matters most on the days it's hardest to say. Day fourteen, done.
